title: Why the Granth is sung
hook: the Gurus set their words in ragas so the music would carry the meaning into the heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ardas, the prayer that remembers the long story before it asks for anything, and your line was the story holds us. A new year starts today, and it starts with sound.

Say a sentence out loud and it's over almost before it starts. Sing the same sentence and it can fill the room for a long while. Nothing in the words has changed, only how long they stay in the room, and where they land. Year four on this path is the ways of the Guru, and it opens with a plain question. The Guru Granth Sahib is scripture. So why did the Gurus write it to be sung?
screen: `SPOKEN, IT'S GONE. SUNG, IT STAYS.` → `YEAR FOUR: THE WAYS OF THE GURU.` → `A BOOK MEANT TO BE SUNG.`

segments.voice: The word is raag, often written raga. Earlier on the path you met it as a mood: a set of notes and a shape of melody that can feel like dusk, or rain, or longing. But first, the why. Above the hymns in the Granth's main body, before the first line, sits the name of a raga. The Gurus didn't leave the tune to chance; they wrote it onto the page, so the words would always arrive with their music. The Granth also says what singing does. In the fifth pauri of the Japji, Guru Nanak puts it in a short chain: sing, listen, and keep love in the mind. Then pain is sent away and peace comes home. Singing and listening stand side by side: one voice sings, and the whole room receives it. Guru Arjan, in a salok in the var of Raag Ramkali, goes further. Blessed, he says in effect, are the beautiful ragas whose singing takes away all thirst. Thirst is the picture: something dry in a person that a sentence on a page doesn't always reach, and a melody can. So when Sikhs gather, the Guru's words are sung in kirtan. The meaning is the same as on the page. But a tune slows the words down, lets a singer return to the line that matters, and lets a listener who can't follow every word still sense where the hymn is going. The tune doesn't replace the word. It carries it. Tomorrow, two small marks in those headings that tell singers how.
screen: `RAAG: A MOOD MADE OF NOTES.` · `THE RAGA WRITTEN ABOVE THE HYMN.` · `SING, LISTEN, KEEP LOVE IN THE MIND.` · then, large: `MUSIC CARRIES THE WORD.`

segments.voice: If you have a recording of a raga played without words, a sitar, a sarangi, a flute, start it softly; if not, hum one low note, or listen to the longest steady sound near you, a fan or a fridge. Don't try to name anything; just follow the sound as it rises and settles, and notice where your attention goes with no sentence to hold. If you pray, let Waheguru ride on the sound once, silently.
Raag. A musical setting with its own notes and mood, written above the Guru's hymns so the words arrive with their music. Today's word.
Your line: music carries the word. A tune slows the words down so they can land. Year four has begun.

howItsDone: In gurdwaras the Guru's hymns are sung as kirtan by ragis and by the congregation, and the raga named in each hymn's heading guides how trained musicians set it.

chat.says: If the Granth is scripture, why do Sikhs sing it instead of just reading it?
options: The Gurus set their words in ragas, named in the headings, so music would carry the meaning.
Singing is a later custom; the Gurus meant their words to be read silently on the page.
The tune changes the meaning, so each singer gives the hymn a new message of their own.
